note: Single source of truth for every metric shown in the portal. The info buttons on the selection panel and the village card read from this file, and the reference table in about.html is generated from it, so the two cannot drift apart.

items.label: Villages
items.what: How many gazette rows are in the current selection.
items.how: One row per village named in Annexure C of the notification that was matched to a boundary. 4,331 of 4,402 rows matched overall.
items.caveat: A few gazette rows name the same place more than once for different survey blocks; the 1:1 constraint gives the polygon to the first, so those repeats appear under Not mapped.

items.label: Total area
items.what: Ground area of the selected village polygons.
items.how: Measured in EPSG:7755, an equal-area projection for India, never in degrees.
items.caveat: Bifurcated and Kerala villages are drawn whole, so this is larger than the area actually notified. Kerala measured against its own official boundary is 8,863 km² rather than 13,030.

items.label: Population
items.what: Resident population of the selected settlements at the 2011 Census.
items.how: Joined on the 2011 census code from both Primary Census Abstracts — the rural village directory and the town/ward directory. 4,330 of 4,331 records match.
items.caveat: This is whole-village population. Where only part of a village was notified, everyone in the village is counted, so treat it as an upper bound. One record, Valvane in Satara, has no census code and no figure.

items.label: Households
items.what: Number of households recorded by the 2011 Census.
items.how: Census field No_HH, summed across the selection.
items.caveat: Same whole-village basis as population.

items.label: Scheduled Tribe
items.what: Residents recorded as Scheduled Tribe.
items.how: Census field P_ST. The percentage is of the selection's total population.
items.caveat: Relevant to Forest Rights Act claims, but the whole-village basis applies here too.

items.label: Density
items.what: How densely settled the selection is.
items.how: Total population divided by total area.
items.caveat: Because the area is whole-village and includes uninhabited forest, density is lower than the lived experience of the settled parts.

items.label: Land-dependent workers
items.what: Share of working people whose livelihood is directly tied to land.
items.how: Cultivators plus agricultural labourers, divided by total workers. Census fields MAIN_CL_P, MAIN_AL_P, TOT_WORK_P.
items.caveat: A measure of who stands to be affected by land-use restrictions, not of poverty.

items.label: Park, sanctuary or ESZ
items.what: How much of the selection already sits inside a National Park, Wildlife Sanctuary, or an Eco-Sensitive Zone notified around one.
items.how: Union of the India-WRIS national protected-area layer and the Parivesh Eco-Sensitive Zone layer, intersected with the villages. Unioned first, because summing per-feature intersections would double-count overlap.
items.caveat: Replaces the OpenStreetMap-derived layer used until v3.10, which carried unquantified error. Two things to know about the new source. India-WRIS (Ministry of Jal Shakti) REPUBLISHES protected-area boundaries; it is not the notifying authority, which is MoEFCC, so this is an official portal’s copy rather than a notified boundary. And its latest year of notification is 2021, so any park, sanctuary or ESZ notified between 2022 and the 2024 draft gazette is missing. The switch moved protection inside the ESA from 15,759 km² (28.0%) to 15,003 km² (26.7%); earlier downloads will not reconcile with current ones. The WII protected-area shapefile was also compared and rejected: it is a mid-2010s snapshot missing Kodaikanal, Megamalai and Bhimgad, and self-overlaps by 3.5%.

items.label: Corridor outside protection
items.what: Corridor land that is NOT already inside a protected area — the ground that connects protected areas rather than forming part of one.
items.how: The Parivesh wildlife-corridor layer with all protected area (parks, sanctuaries and Eco-Sensitive Zones) subtracted. Protection is removed rather than overlaid, so this figure and the protection figure are disjoint and may be added.
items.caveat: The subtraction removes 53% of the raw corridor layer as already protected. It also repairs a defect in the source: that layer’s type field files national parks and sanctuaries as "corridor" — Bandipur, Periyar and Parambikulam among them — and 79% of its "tiger reserve" area also sat inside its "corridor" area. Read this as POLICY OVERLAP, not as measured ecological connectivity: it records whether an identified corridor crosses the village, not how much movement the village actually carries. A sole pinch-point and the ragged edge of a wide corridor score the same per unit area; nothing here is least-cost or circuit-modelled. It is zero for 78% of villages, and for that reason it is NOT a component of the conservation score — it is published, mapped and filterable only.

items.label: Tiger reserve
items.what: Village area inside a tiger reserve.
items.how: Those India-WRIS protected areas whose sub-type field marks them as part of a tiger reserve, intersected with the villages.
items.caveat: This is the protected-area CORE of each reserve, not the full notified reserve. A tiger reserve is core plus buffer, and buffer zones are frequently not themselves notified parks or sanctuaries, so they are absent here — against NTCA’s notified totals these polygons run roughly half. It is a subset of the protection figure, never an addition to it: the source layer is de-overlapped, so every tiger-reserve polygon is also a protected-area polygon. Cross-checked against the WII tiger-reserve layer, which agrees to within 1% inside the ESA (5,471 km² against 5,409 km²). The WII layer used for that cross-check is itself a core-only tiger-reserve layer, so the agreement confirms the core extent, not the full notified reserve.

items.label: Recorded Forest Area
items.what: Land already recorded as forest, and so already under forest administration.
items.how: The Bharatmaps Recorded Forest Area layer intersected with the villages, unioned first.
items.caveat: Where the ESA overlaps recorded forest, the notification changes relatively little — the state already controls land use there.

items.label: Outside Recorded Forest
items.what: The remainder: village area not recorded as forest.
items.how: Total area minus Recorded Forest Area.
items.caveat: This is NOT private land. It also holds revenue and common land, water bodies, PSU and defence land, and gaps in the forest layer itself — 346 villages record no forest area despite being more than half forest. Do not quote it as a private-ownership figure.

items.label: Neither recorded forest nor protected
items.what: Village area that is outside Recorded Forest Area AND outside every park, sanctuary and Eco-Sensitive Zone — the ground where the ESA notification would be the only instrument in force.
items.how: Total area minus the area of the UNION of the recorded-forest and protected layers. It must be measured on the union: most Western Ghats parks are also recorded forest, so subtracting the two figures from each other in turn removes the same ground twice. Until v3.11 it was computed that way and read 18,134 km²; measured correctly it is 20,153 km².
items.caveat: This is NOT private land, and the name is not a description of ownership. It includes water bodies and reservoirs, revenue and common land, PSU and defence land, and every gap in the recorded-forest layer — 346 villages record no forest area despite being more than half forest. A water-body deduction that used to be applied was removed in v3.11 because it double-subtracted; reservoirs are therefore inside this figure. Do not quote it as a private-ownership or an available-land figure.

items.label: Natural forest
items.what: Share under evergreen, semi-evergreen or deciduous forest.
items.how: Categorical zonal statistics over the NRSC LULC 250K 2017-18 raster at 56 m, counted in the raster's own projection so no pixels are resampled. Aggregates are area-weighted.
items.caveat: Mapped at 1:250,000 with 112–168 m registration error. For a village under about 25 km² that band is comparable to its whole area, so those figures are indicative only.

items.label: Plantation
items.what: Agricultural plantation — coffee, cardamom, rubber, tea.
items.how: LULC class 7, distinct from the forest classes.
items.caveat: This is the estate-versus-forest distinction that drives most local opposition. It is published and mappable but deliberately excluded from the composite scores.

items.label: Agriculture
items.what: Cropland and fallow.
items.how: LULC kharif, rabi, zaid, double/triple crop and current fallow classes combined.
items.caveat: Same 1:250,000 scale limit.

items.label: Degraded forest
items.what: Forest land classed as degraded.
items.how: NRSC Wasteland Atlas 2015-16, class 6. The wasteland raster is sparse, so shares are expressed against village area from the land-cover raster, not against the wasteland total.
items.caveat: A different epoch from the land-cover layer (2015-16 against 2017-18).

items.label: Built-up
items.what: Settlement and other built surface.
items.how: LULC class 1.
items.caveat: At 56 m with 1:250,000 mapping, small hamlets fall below what can be resolved.

items.label: Reliable at this scale
items.what: How many villages in the selection are large enough for land cover to be dependable.
items.how: Villages of 25 km² or more. Only 416 of 4,331 clear that bar, though they hold 52% of the area.
items.caveat: Superseded in v3.12 by "Land cover dependable here", which uses the 24 m FSI mapping and a 1 km² floor. This 25 km² figure still applies to the NRSC-derived classes (plantation, agriculture, built-up, grassland), which have no finer equivalent.

items.label: Scrub land
items.what: Land the Wasteland Atlas classes as scrub.
items.how: NRSC Wasteland Atlas 2015-16, class 2. The wasteland raster is sparse, so shares are expressed against village area from the land-cover raster, not against the wasteland total.
items.caveat: The largest wasteland class in the Western Ghats — 4,431 km² across 2,496 villages. Treat the label with care: scrub in the Ghats includes savanna and open natural ecosystems that are habitats in their own right, not degraded forest. "Wasteland" is an administrative category, not an ecological verdict.

items.label: Degraded pasture
items.what: Grazing land classed as degraded.
items.how: NRSC Wasteland Atlas 2015-16, class 7.
items.caveat: Only 405 km² across 52 villages, so it is a local rather than a regional signal. Same labelling caution as scrub land.

items.label: Barren rocky
items.what: Exposed rock and barren ground.
items.how: NRSC Wasteland Atlas 2015-16, class 8.
items.caveat: In the high Ghats this includes rocky plateaux and lateritic outcrops that carry endemic seasonal flora — genuinely bare ground and ecologically distinctive habitat are not separable here.

items.label: Mining / industrial wasteland
items.what: Derelict mining and industrial land.
items.how: NRSC Wasteland Atlas 2015-16, class 1.
items.caveat: This is ABANDONED land as of 2015-16, not active leases. It totals 15 km² across the whole ESA — far too little to represent live extraction in the Goa–Sindhudurg belt. Do not read it as a map of mining activity. Excluded from the scores for the same reason.

items.label: Classed as wasteland
items.what: All Wasteland Atlas classes combined — how much of the selection the government’s wasteland mapping covers.
items.how: Sum of every Wasteland Atlas 2015-16 class present, each measured against village area from the land-cover raster. Dominated by degraded forest (6,762 km²) and scrub land (4,431 km²); the remaining eight classes total under 800 km².
items.caveat: 11,973 km² — 21.3% of the proposed ESA — carries a "wasteland" label. That is a land-revenue classification with a long history of marking open natural ecosystems as unproductive, and it sits awkwardly beside the same ground being proposed for ecological protection. Published so the tension is visible, not because the label is endorsed. A different epoch from the land-cover layer (2015-16 against 2017-18).

items.label: Forest cover (FSI)
items.what: Tree canopy cover of 10% or more, as the Forest Survey of India maps it.
items.how: FSI forest-cover raster, ISFR 2019 cycle, at 24 m: open (10–40% canopy) plus moderately dense (40–70%) plus very dense (≥70%). Counted in the raster’s own projection so no pixels are resampled.
items.caveat: A different question from "natural forest", not a better answer to the same one. FSI measures canopy density and counts plantations, coffee and rubber as forest; the NRSC land-cover measure separates them. Across the ESA the two agree closely — 72.1% against 71.8% — but they part company in 47 villages that average 59.5% plantation. Both are published so the disagreement is visible.

items.label: Dense + moderate canopy
items.what: Forest with a closed or near-closed canopy — 40% cover and above.
items.how: FSI ISFR 2019 moderately dense (40–70%) plus very dense (≥70%) classes. Across the ESA: 22,479 km² moderately dense and 7,557 km² very dense, 53.4% of the area.
items.caveat: This is the structural-condition half of the conservation score’s forest component. Before FSI was added the score could not tell 90% open forest from 90% very dense forest. It still counts plantation canopy as forest, which is why it is averaged with the natural-forest measure rather than used alone.

items.label: Very dense forest
items.what: Canopy cover of 70% or above.
items.how: FSI ISFR 2019, class 6. 7,557 km² across the ESA, 13.4% of the area.
items.caveat: Mapped at 24 m, so unlike the 1:250,000 land-cover layer this is dependable for small villages.

items.label: Open forest
items.what: Canopy cover between 10% and 40%.
items.how: FSI ISFR 2019, class 4. 10,533 km², 18.7% of the ESA.
items.caveat: Open canopy can mean naturally open woodland or degraded closed forest; the class does not distinguish them.

items.label: Land cover dependable here
items.what: How many villages in the selection are large enough for land-cover figures to be trusted.
items.how: Villages of 1 km² or more. FSI 2019 is mapped at 24 m, so the size floor is about 1 km² rather than the 25 km² the 1:250,000 NRSC layer needed: 4,203 of 4,331 villages clear it, against 416 before.
items.caveat: The NRSC-derived figures on this page — plantation, agriculture, built-up, grassland — still carry the coarser 1:250,000 limit, because no 24 m equivalent exists for those classes. Only the FSI canopy measures gain the finer floor.

items.label: National highway
items.what: Length of national highway running inside the selection.
items.how: MoRTH highway network from GatiShakti, clipped to the village polygons.
items.caveat: National highways only — state highways and district roads are not included, so this understates road presence.

items.label: Conservation value
items.what: How much forest a village holds and how much of it is already recorded forest. Read the caveat before calling it ecological value.
items.how: Mean of two percentile-ranked components. The first is forest, measured by two independent sensors and averaged: NRSC land cover for forest TYPE (evergreen and deciduous, excluding plantation) and FSI ISFR 2019 for canopy DENSITY (dense and moderately dense, including plantation). The second is Recorded Forest Area %, which is tenure.
items.caveat: A percentile rank against the other ESA villages, not an absolute measure. Understand what it does and does not contain. Both components describe forest: natural forest % is measured from imagery, Recorded Forest Area % is tenure status, so this is closer to "forest cover and forest tenure" than to a biodiversity score. It contains no measure of endemism, irreplaceability or spatial configuration, which is what systematic conservation prioritisation normally rests on. A band of "low priority" therefore means low forest cover and non-forest tenure — not low ecological value. Note also that natural forest % counts evergreen and deciduous forest only, so montane grassland (170 km² of the ESA), scrub forest (699 km²) and littoral swamp score zero on it, and the shola–grassland mosaic and Myristica swamps are under-valued despite being among the most endemic-rich habitats in the range; the broader forest_pct field is published for anyone who wants them included. A corridor component was removed in v3.11 after an audit — it was zero for 78% of villages, so percentile-ranking turned it into a flag, and being the complement of protection it pushed protected villages down while recorded forest pushed them up. Of the two survivors, natural forest % is a clean gradient (1.8% zeros, 3,347 distinct values) and Recorded Forest Area % carries a 17.5% tie block at zero.

items.label: Human pressure
items.what: Where restrictions will be felt most.
items.how: Mean of four percentile-ranked components: population density, built-up %, highway density per km², and land-dependent workers %.
items.caveat: Deliberately measures people and infrastructure only. An earlier version shared variables with the conservation score, which forced 86% of villages onto one diagonal; the two now correlate −0.48.

items.label: Priority bands
items.what: Where each village falls on the two axes together.
items.how: Both scores cut into terciles, giving nine cells, each separately named: protect, protect with some pressure, negotiate, secondary, moderate on both, pressure-led, low priority, contested.
items.caveat: Terciles are relative to this dataset. **The bands changed in v3.11**: removing the corridor component from the conservation score moved 770 of 4,331 villages (17.8%) across a band boundary, so a band cited from an earlier download may not match the current one. An earlier version named only three cells and dumped 59% of villages into an uninformative "mixed".

items.label: Literacy
items.what: Literate residents as a share of population.
items.how: Census field P_LIT divided by total population.
items.caveat: Census definition of literacy, age 7 and above.

items.label: Gazette entry
items.what: How the village appears in the notification itself, before any processing.
items.how: State, district, taluka, village name and serial number transcribed from Annexure C, plus the verbatim printed form including the * bifurcation marker.
items.caveat: The gazette's district and taluka names are sometimes older than the census ones — Surat and Tapi, for instance.

items.label: Name match score
items.what: How confidently the gazette name was matched to a census village.
items.how: RapidFuzz similarity after transliteration folding, with the scope showing how wide the search had to go: district+taluka, district, or state-wide.
items.caveat: A low score, or a state-wide scope, means the pairing deserves checking against the gazette.

items.label: Setting
items.what: Which forest and hydrological units the village sits in.
items.how: Largest-overlap assignment against FSI forest divisions and ranges, and India-WRIS river basins and sub-basins.
items.caveat: A location label only. Nothing here measures water yield or forest administration workload.
